To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) people's responses are influenced by the way questions are asked; (b) the effects are systematic and predictable; (c) the underlying processes can be understood; (d) these processes can be manipulated to improve the quality of data; and (e) these processes are not unique to surveys, but also operate in other contexts, including everyday conversation.

(1) the way a question is asked influences the way it is answered, (2) the influence of question wording on the answers is systematic, (3) question comprehension is the key to understanding the influence of question features, and (4) context effects are a pervasive feature of self-reports.
the answers to survey questions are influenced by the way the questions are phrased and by the way they are asked.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what people know, how they think, and what they do when they answer questions.
how people understand and answer questions, not how to manipulate their responses.
the cognitive and communicative underpinnings of survey questions, and the implications of these processes for questionnaire design and the interpretation of self-report measures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
self-reports are not only a source of information about the respondent but also a source of information for the researcher about the respondent's cognitive and communicative behavior.
self-reports are not always valid, but they can be valid, and they are the only practical way of obtaining information about private events.
the questions shape the self-reports.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more we know about the underlying processes, the more we know how to design questions that will elicit accurate answers.
the questions shape the responses.
the questions shape the answer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
self-reports are not a single method, but a set of methods with different strengths and weaknesses.
the research instrument can be used to shape the answers, but that the instrument can also be used to improve the quality of the answers.

the research instrument can have a profound impact on self-reports, and that the instrument is not just a passive conduit of respondents' true beliefs, but an active shaper of the responses that are given.
